items.title: 53 Interviews, One Toxic Verdict: What the Watchdog Report on Ex-Labor Secretary Chavez-DeRemer Found
items.body:
A long-awaited watchdog report has laid out a detailed account of misconduct allegations against former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, describing a workplace culture that dozens of current and former staffers called "toxic, intimidating and humiliating" in the months before she stepped down.

The report, released by the Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General, caps a months-long investigation that began after the OIG received an anonymous complaint about conditions inside the secretary's office. Chavez-DeRemer resigned from her post in April, and the 44-page findings were only made public this week following pressure from congressional Democrats who had pushed the department to release them.

## How the Investigation Was Conducted

According to the report, investigators interviewed 53 current and former Labor Department employees, along with one staffer from another federal agency, and reviewed more than 500 documents, images and videos, including surveillance footage, as part of the inquiry. The probe was led by a former member of Congress serving in an oversight capacity within the department.

Of those interviewed, 38 described the atmosphere inside the secretary's office in similarly negative terms, telling investigators that performance reviews were sometimes discussed openly in front of other staff — including, in some accounts, whether employees had been reduced to tears in meetings. Witnesses said the environment fostered "widespread fear and job insecurity," with several employees reporting they had been threatened with termination.

## What the Report Alleges

Investigators say the evidence pointed to misconduct across several distinct areas. Per the report, Chavez-DeRemer is alleged to have:

- Contributed to a hostile work environment within the department
- Engaged in an inappropriate relationship with a member of her security detail
- Failed to comply with established federal travel regulations, including use of government resources for personal trips
- Consumed alcohol in Labor Department offices or during duty hours on multiple occasions
- Directed subordinates to carry out tasks for her personal benefit
- Accepted gifts without reporting them through the department's required ethics channels

The Inspector General's office said the findings were based on a preponderance of witness testimony and documentary evidence gathered over the course of the investigation.

## The Response

An attorney representing Chavez-DeRemer pushed back on the report's conclusions, saying she "did not violate any law" and criticizing what the attorney described as premature speculation that had circulated before the findings were made public. Chavez-DeRemer has not been charged with any crime, and the OIG report is an administrative review rather than a criminal referral.

The Labor Department has not announced any further disciplinary or legal action tied to the findings. It remains unclear whether the report will be referred to any additional oversight body for review.

## Why It Matters

The episode adds to a string of personnel controversies that surfaced at the department during Chavez-DeRemer's tenure, including the earlier departures of two top aides amid the same internal investigation. Lawmakers on the House and Senate labor committees have signaled they may seek additional briefings on the report's findings, and government watchdog groups have pointed to the case as a test of how executive agencies handle misconduct complaints against their own leadership.

For now, the report stands as a formal, if belated, accounting of what investigators say went on behind closed doors at one of the government's largest agencies — and a reminder that inspector general offices, however slow-moving, remain one of the few internal checks on how cabinet-level officials conduct themselves in office.

items.title: Four Dead, One Alleged Drone: Inside the Israeli Strikes Testing Lebanon's Fragile Truce
items.body:
## A Deadly Exchange in South Lebanon

Israeli airstrikes killed four people in southern Lebanon, the country's health ministry reported, after the Israeli military said the operation was carried out in response to a drone launched from Lebanese territory toward Israel. The strikes mark one of the more serious escalations since a ceasefire arrangement between Israel and Hezbollah took hold, and they underscore how easily the current calm along the border can be shaken.

The Israeli military said its aircraft targeted what it described as sites and individuals linked to Hezbollah's efforts to rebuild military infrastructure in the south, an area where the group's armed presence is supposed to be curtailed under the terms worked out after the last major round of fighting. Lebanese authorities have not independently confirmed the drone launch that Israel cited as the trigger for its response, and Hezbollah has not issued a detailed public accounting of the incident.

## Why the Truce Keeps Cracking

The ceasefire that ended the most intense phase of the Israel-Hezbollah conflict was never a full peace agreement. It was built around a framework, reaffirmed in talks over the summer, meant to gradually push Hezbollah's fighters and weapons north of the Litani River while Israel withdrew from positions it had held inside Lebanon. Monitoring was left to a mechanism involving the Lebanese army, United Nations peacekeepers (UNIFIL), and international observers, including the United States and France.

In practice, that structure has been tested repeatedly. Israel has continued carrying out strikes it says are aimed at preventing Hezbollah from restocking weapons or restoring command infrastructure, arguing that the group has not fully complied with disarmament commitments. Lebanese officials and Hezbollah, in turn, have accused Israel of violating the truce through strikes that go beyond narrow counterterrorism aims, including hits near populated areas and on infrastructure they say has no military value.

Each side interprets the same set of events differently: Israel frames its strikes as necessary enforcement of the deal, while Lebanese officials describe many of them as violations of Lebanese sovereignty. That gap in interpretation, rather than any single incident, is what analysts point to as the truce's core vulnerability.

## What Comes Next

For residents of southern Lebanon, the practical effect is a return to daily uncertainty. Villages that had begun to see displaced families return since the ceasefire are once again grappling with the sound of airstrikes and the risk that a single contested incident, like an alleged drone launch, can trigger a broader exchange.

Diplomats involved in sustaining the framework, including U.S. and French officials who helped broker it, are expected to press both sides to stick to the agreed channels for reporting and verifying incidents rather than resorting immediately to strikes or retaliatory attacks. Whether that pressure holds may determine if this latest episode remains an isolated flare-up or becomes the moment the broader truce starts to unravel.

For now, Lebanese officials have called for calm and urged an independent review of what actually happened before the strikes, while Israeli officials maintain their action was a proportionate response to a direct threat. With both governments continuing to affirm they want the ceasefire to hold, the coming days are likely to show whether that shared interest is strong enough to absorb another shock.
